talks.title: Dan Petro and Oscar Salaza - Hacking Smart Safes: On the Brink of a Robbery
talks.teaser: Dan Petro and Oscar Salazar reverse engineer electronic smart safes, uncovering firmware vulnerabilities and remote lock bypasses.
talks.summary:
The Anatomy of Commercial Smart Safes

Dan Petro and Oscar Salazar examine the security architecture of commercial "smart safes" deployed in retail businesses, restaurants, and financial branches. These connected safes combine physical armored vaults with digital bill validators, touchscreen management terminals, and network reporting interfaces to streamline cash handling.

Hardware Reverse Engineering and Bus Sniffing

The researchers reverse engineer several leading smart safe platforms, analyzing communication between the main computing unit, internal logic boards, and electronic lock solenoids. By tapping serial buses and inspecting PCB traces with logic analyzers, the authors uncover unencrypted internal communication channels carrying plaintext control commands.

Extracting Administrative Credentials and Solenoid Actuation

Petro and Salazar demonstrate multiple attack vectors, including sniffing supervisory PINs directly from ribbon cables and injecting malicious commands via exposed external USB ports. Using a custom microcontroller payload (Teensy), the researchers execute automated scripts that trigger the electronic lock solenoids, opening the physical safe vault in seconds.

Remediation and Embedded Physical Security Design

The presentation outlines critical engineering guidelines for electronic safe manufacturers. Securing connected physical security devices requires implementing end-to-end cryptographic authentication across internal component buses, disabling external debugging ports, and ensuring physical tamper detection circuitry cannot be bypassed externally.

talks.title: AmmonRa - How to Hack Your Way out of Home Detention
talks.teaser: Analyzing the radio frequency signals, tamper sensors, and hardware limitations of electronic home detention and ankle monitoring bracelets.
talks.summary:
Architecture of Electronic Home Confinement Systems

Security researcher AmmonRa analyzes electronic monitoring systems used by judicial systems for home detention, curfew enforcement, and parole monitoring. These systems typically comprise a tamper-resistant radio-frequency ankle bracelet paired with a localized base station that reports telemetry to monitoring centers via cellular GSM networks.

RF Proximity Signaling and Base Station Interception

AmmonRa examines the wireless communication between the ankle bracelet and the base station, exploring how proximity is determined through periodic radio beacons. By reverse engineering the RF signaling characteristics, the researcher evaluates whether beacon signals can be captured and spoofed to simulate presence while leaving the designated confinement perimeter.

Cellular Telemetry and Protocol Weaknesses

The presentation investigates the base station's communication back to judicial monitoring facilities, focusing on SMS and cellular data channels. AmmonRa uncovers unauthenticated protocol structures, predictable device identifiers, and insecure remote configuration interfaces that could permit an attacker to spoof status reports or suppress tamper alerts.

Forensic Realities and the Risks of Tampering

While technical attack vectors exist in legacy monitoring architectures, AmmonRa emphasizes the extensive physical tamper detection mechanisms—including fiber-optic strap loops, skin-temperature sensors, and motion sensors—engineered into modern hardware. The talk concludes with a discussion of ethical and legal implications, highlighting design weaknesses while discouraging criminal exploitation.
